one_liner: Header-only C++ algebraic multigrid solver library; sets up AMG preconditioners faster than Trilinos ML and PETSc GAMG on shared memory.
what_it_does: Solves large sparse linear systems Ax=b with Krylov solvers (CG, BiCGStab, GMRES, ...) preconditioned by algebraic multigrid, without needing mesh geometry. Solvers are composed at compile time from policy templates (amgcl::make_solver<amgcl::amg<Backend, Coarsening, Relaxation>, Solver>) or at runtime through a Boost.property_tree interface; parameters live in nested params structs. Input matrices can be CRS tuples, Eigen::SparseMatrix, Epetra_CrsMatrix or any type with adapter free functions; MPI versions are provided for distributed memory.
how_it_is_fast: The AMG hierarchy (e.g. smoothed aggregation coarsening) is built on the CPU with OpenMP using shared-memory data structures, avoiding the distributed-memory bookkeeping that the docs blame for PETSc's and Trilinos' slower setup. After setup the hierarchy is moved to a backend (builtin OpenMP, CUDA/cuSPARSE, VexCL/OpenCL, ViennaCL, HIP), so the solve phase runs on GPUs transparently. Cheap default smoothers (SPAI0) and static block value types (e.g. 4x4 blocks) cut setup cost and memory traffic; Schur pressure-correction field-split preconditioners handle coupled systems like Navier-Stokes.
when_to_use: Single-node solves of large elliptic/PDE systems (millions of unknowns) where you rebuild the preconditioner often and setup time matters.
C++ codes that want an AMG preconditioner without adopting PETSc or Trilinos data structures or build systems.
Solve-heavy workloads on a GPU (CUDA, OpenCL, HIP) where solution phase alone was 3-4x faster than CPU on the docs' Poisson test.
Block-structured systems (elasticity, Navier-Stokes) using static block value types or field-split Schur pressure correction.
Mixed precision or custom value types via template specialization.
when_not_to_use: Large distributed-memory runs: the project's own weak-scaling test shows AMGCL about 3x slower than Trilinos AMG, and PETSc scales better than both on shared memory.
You need a direct solver or robust black-box behaviour on hard indefinite or highly anisotropic problems; open issues report convergence trouble on a 3D structural problem (#300).
Total time-to-solution on GPU for one-shot solves: setup always runs on the CPU, so CUDA total time was only about 30% better than OpenMP AMGCL.
32-bit targets (open i386 build failure, #312) or very large CUDA problems (int overflow, #287).
Strict bitwise reproducibility across thread counts unless you define AMGCL_DETERMINISTIC_REDUCTIONS (may be slower on many cores).

integration.dependencies: OpenMP (recommended); Boost.property_tree only for the runtime interface (removable with AMGCL_NO_BOOST); per-backend extras: CUDA/cuSPARSE/Thrust, VexCL (Boost + OpenCL/CUDA), ViennaCL, ROCm hipSPARSE/rocSPARSE; MPI 3.0 for distributed solvers; optional Eigen, METIS/Scotch, PaStiX
integration.min_toolchain: C++ standard not documented for the core; CMake 3.10+ for the bundled build; HIP backend requires C++17
integration.platforms: any with a C++ compiler (GCC, Clang, Intel, MSVC configured in CMake); GPUs via CUDA, OpenCL or HIP; i386 build currently broken per open issue
integration.thread_safety: not documented (setup and builtin backend are internally OpenMP-parallel)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces PETSc/Trilinos ML AMG preconditioning with a different C++ template API; adapters accept CRS arrays, Eigen and Epetra matrices, but solver options and defaults differ

gotchas: Benchmarks compare each library on its default smoother (AMGCL SPAI0, Trilinos symmetric Gauss-Seidel, PETSc damped Jacobi), so iteration counts and solve time are not like-for-like.
OpenMP reductions give last-bit differences with different thread counts by default; define AMGCL_DETERMINISTIC_REDUCTIONS to fix.
Heavy template composition means long compile times and large binaries (MSVC needs /bigobj, set by the CMake target).
Open issue #291 reports growing memory when called repeatedly from a pybind11 module.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick AMGCL over Ginkgo when you want a small header-only AMG with fast CPU setup and runtime-configurable solvers; pick Ginkgo for GPU-first sparse work where its AMG beat NVIDIA AmgX. Unlike BaSpaCho or Sympiler (direct Cholesky), AMGCL is iterative and suits very large PDE systems where factorization fill-in is too costly.
verified_claims_summary: On a dual Xeon E5-2640 v3 node, solving a 3D Poisson finite-difference system (3,375,000 unknowns, 23.5M nonzeros) with AMG-preconditioned CG, the author's docs report AMGCL (OpenMP) setup about 20-100% faster than Trilinos ML and 4-7x faster than PETSc (both via MPI), with overall CPU time on par with Trilinos; a Tesla K80 CUDA run cut solve time 3-4x but total time only about 30%. Compiler and flags are not stated.
status_note: Actively maintained (release 1.4.9 in June 2026, 871 stars, 59 open issues), MIT-licensed and header-only, so easy to vendor.
